introduction-why-platforms-need-devrel.core: Great platform features fail silently if developers don't know about them, don't trust them or can't get help. Internal DevRel builds awareness, education, trust and feedback loops between the platform team and its users.

first_principles.problem: A platform ships powerful self-service features that few teams discover, so adoption lags and duplicate tools spread.

analogy.title: A new highway with no signs
analogy.story: Commuters keep taking the old roads because nobody told them, or showed them, the new route.
analogy.breaks: DevRel can't save a bad product, so quality comes first.

example.title: Two identical features
flow: DevRel: demo, guide, office hours, champions → 55%

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The same feature, much more impact.

example.outcome: platform features that reach their users.

check.q: Why do internal platforms need DevRel?
check.a: Without awareness, education and trust, even great features go unused.

internal-evangelism-strategies.core: Internal evangelists are trusted by both platform and product teams. They speak developers' language, demo real use cases, write tutorials, recruit champions and represent user needs back to the platform team. Credibility comes from being hands-on and honest.

first_principles.problem: Platform announcements read like marketing and are ignored by sceptical engineers.
derivation: Build a **champions network** inside product teams.
Be **honest** about gaps; advocate for users internally.

analogy.title: A trusted local guide
analogy.story: Visitors trust the guide who knows the city and is honest about which streets to avoid.
analogy.breaks: Evangelists who only cheerlead lose credibility, so represent users truthfully.

check.q: What makes an internal evangelist credible to engineers?
check.a: Hands-on expertise, real demos and honesty about the platform's limitations.

office-hours-and-hackathons.core: High-touch engagement builds trust faster than docs: office hours answer questions people didn't know to ask and surface friction, while hackathons and onboarding workshops get teams hands-on with the platform alongside the platform engineers.

first_principles.problem: Developers struggle silently with the platform because asking feels like bothering the platform team.
derivation: Run **migration hackathons**: teams migrate with experts present.
**Log** questions to improve docs and the product.

analogy.title: A teacher's office hours and lab sessions
analogy.story: Students learn far more from questions answered in person and guided lab work than from the textbook alone.
analogy.breaks: This doesn't scale infinitely, so convert recurring questions into docs and features.

example.title: A migration hackathon
flow: 9 services migrated by end of day

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Adoption leaps, and product feedback piles up.

example.outcome: trust and adoption through direct contact.

check.q: Why are office hours valuable even with good documentation?
check.a: They surface hidden friction and answer questions people didn't know to ask, while building trust.

measuring-success-the-developer-nps-and-.core: Measure DevRel through developer NPS ('How likely are you to recommend the platform to a colleague?'), satisfaction by feature, adoption funnels, office-hour themes, docs usage and support ticket trends, so you know whether relationships and sentiment are improving.

first_principles.problem: DevRel work feels intangible, and the team can't show its impact.
truths: Funnels show where users drop off.
derivation: Run a **quarterly NPS survey** with open comments.

analogy.title: A restaurant tracking reviews and repeat visits
analogy.story: Ratings and returning diners tell you whether the experience is improving.
analogy.breaks: NPS is a blunt instrument, so read the comments, not just the score.

check.a: How likely developers are to recommend the platform to colleagues, a proxy for satisfaction and advocacy.

building-a-feedback-culture-closing-the-.core: Collecting feedback is easy; the underrated part is visibly acting on it and telling people. 'You said, we did' changelogs, public feedback boards and follow-ups show users their input matters, which earns more and better feedback.

first_principles.problem: Developers fill in surveys and file requests that disappear into a void, so they stop giving feedback.
truths: People give feedback when they see impact.
derivation: Collect it in **one place** (feedback board, issues).
**Triage** and respond to every item, even with 'not now'.
**Follow up** with the people who asked.

analogy.title: A town council's suggestion box
analogy.story: If suggestions visibly lead to changes, with credit given, residents keep contributing.
analogy.breaks: You can't build everything, so explaining 'no' honestly also builds trust.

example.title: A 'you said, we did' update
flow: You said: CI too slow → we added caching (−40%)
You said: unclear errors → rewrote 30 messages
You said: need Python template → shipped
example.outcome: users who feel heard and stay engaged.

check.q: What does 'closing the loop' mean in feedback culture?
check.a: Visibly acting on feedback and telling the people who gave it what changed (or why not).
